cards.statement: A transit gateway uses route propagation to choose the lookup table for traffic entering from a VPC attachment.
cards.explanation: A transit gateway looks up incoming traffic in the route table associated with the ingress attachment. Propagation installs an attachment's routes in selected tables.
cards.misconception: Route propagation selects the lookup table for traffic arriving on an attachment.

source.title: How AWS Transit Gateway works

cards.statement: With one transit gateway per appliance VPC, appliance mode keeps a VPC-to-VPC flow in one inspection Availability Zone.
cards.explanation: AWS Transit Gateway appliance mode keeps both flow directions on the same inspection VPC interface when one transit gateway connects to that VPC.

source.title: How AWS Transit Gateway works

cards.statement: Within a Region, a transit gateway peered with an AWS Cloud WAN core network learns routes through BGP.
cards.explanation: AWS Cloud WAN peering dynamically exchanges routes between transit gateway route tables and core network segments, preserving the configured segmentation.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Cloud WAN peering capabilities are evolving.

source.title: Peerings in AWS Cloud WAN

cards.statement: AWS PrivateLink can fail over a cross-Region endpoint to an endpoint service in a different service Region.
cards.explanation: For cross-Region access, AWS PrivateLink handles Availability Zone failover. The architect provides recovery across service Regions.
cards.misconception: Cross-Region connectivity includes failover to a service in another Region.
cards.volatilityNote: Cross-Region AWS PrivateLink resilience capabilities may expand.

source.title: Share your services through AWS PrivateLink

cards.statement: A central network account can associate its Direct Connect gateway with a transit gateway in another account.
cards.explanation: The transit gateway owner proposes the association, and the Direct Connect gateway owner accepts it to connect the attached VPCs to the central hybrid network.

source.title: Direct Connect gateways

cards.statement: AWS Direct Connect MACsec encrypts traffic end to end from the customer router to resources in a VPC.
cards.explanation: Direct Connect MACsec protects the cross-connect between the customer's router and the Direct Connect router. Its protection ends at that Ethernet link.
cards.misconception: MACsec encryption extends across the AWS network to the workload.

source.title: MAC Security in Direct Connect

cards.statement: Route 53 VPC Resolver can forward corporate DNS queries from several accounts through shared forwarding rules.
cards.explanation: Route 53 VPC Resolver uses an outbound endpoint to reach corporate DNS servers. Shared Resolver rules reuse that forwarding configuration across accounts.

source.title: What is Route 53 VPC Resolver?

cards.statement: For the same domain, a Route 53 Profile's private hosted zone overrides one associated directly with the VPC.
cards.explanation: When a query matches a private hosted zone associated directly with the VPC and one associated through its Route 53 Profile, the VPC's local setting wins; otherwise the most specific domain name wins.
cards.misconception: A Route 53 Profile's private hosted zone takes precedence over a zone associated directly with the VPC for the same domain.

source.title: What are Amazon Route 53 Profiles?

cards.statement: A participant account can update route tables in a VPC subnet that the network account shares through AWS RAM.
cards.explanation: The VPC owner manages the shared subnet's route tables. Participant accounts can describe them but cannot create, change, or associate them.
cards.misconception: Sharing a subnet delegates routing control to participant accounts.

source.title: Responsibilities and permissions for owners and participants

cards.statement: Reachability Analyzer can model a cross-account VPC path to locate network configuration blocking traffic.
cards.explanation: Reachability Analyzer models routes and network controls instead of sending packets. It can analyze connected VPCs across accounts in one Region within an organization.

source.title: How Reachability Analyzer works

cards.statement: An IAM Identity Center account instance grants workforce access to accounts across an organization.
cards.explanation: IAM Identity Center requires an organization instance for multi-account workforce access. An account instance serves isolated AWS managed application deployments.
cards.misconception: An account instance provides organization-wide AWS account access.

source.title: Organization and account instances of IAM Identity Center

cards.statement: Account access manager can assign existing IAM roles to IAM Identity Center users across an organization.
cards.explanation: Account access manager maps existing account roles to workforce users and groups. Teams retain their custom roles while managing assignments centrally.
cards.volatilityNote: Account access manager is a recently introduced account-access capability.

source.title: Account access manager

cards.statement: Policy-based cross-account AWS KMS decryption needs an Allow in the key policy and the caller's IAM policy.
cards.explanation: Policy-based AWS KMS access across accounts combines the key owner's policy with permission delegated through IAM in the caller's account.

source.title: Allowing users in other accounts to use a KMS key

cards.statement: AWS KMS automatically applies a primary key's policy updates to related multi-Region replica keys.
cards.explanation: Related multi-Region keys have independent key policies. Administrators maintain authorization in each Region because AWS KMS does not synchronize those policies.
cards.misconception: KMS synchronizes authorization policies with shared multi-Region key properties.

source.title: Control access to multi-Region keys

cards.statement: A GuardDuty delegated administrator designated in one Region manages member accounts only in that Region.
cards.explanation: GuardDuty administration is Regional: the delegated administrator and its members are added in each Region where GuardDuty is enabled, and the same account must be the administrator in every Region.

source.title: Managing GuardDuty accounts with AWS Organizations

cards.statement: Member account administrators can change event selection on their AWS CloudTrail organization trail.
cards.explanation: Member administrators can inspect a CloudTrail organization trail, but its configuration remains under the management account or CloudTrail delegated administrator's control.
cards.misconception: Member-account administrative access includes changing the organization trail.

source.title: Creating a trail for an organization

cards.statement: Application Load Balancers in different Regions can reference the same AWS Certificate Manager certificate ARN.
cards.explanation: Certificates in AWS Certificate Manager are Regional resources. Load balancers in different Regions require certificate resources in their respective Regions.
cards.misconception: An ACM certificate resource is usable by load balancers across Regions.

source.title: Import certificates into AWS Certificate Manager

cards.statement: AWS Security Hub can aggregate member-account findings from linked Regions into its administrator's home Region.
cards.explanation: Member accounts inherit their administrator's aggregation settings. Security Hub replicates their findings from linked Regions into the home Region for central visibility.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Security Hub's unified service and aggregation capabilities are evolving.

source.title: Understanding cross-Region aggregation in Security Hub

cards.statement: IAM Identity Center lets administrators edit multi-account permission sets through an additional Region.
cards.explanation: IAM Identity Center administrators manage multi-account permission sets in the primary Region. Additional Regions replicate account access rather than offering another administration location.
cards.misconception: Identity Center replication makes permission-set administration writable in additional Regions.
cards.volatilityNote: IAM Identity Center multi-Region replication is a recently introduced capability.

source.title: Availability of IAM Identity Center use cases in the primary and additional Regions

cards.statement: An AWS warm standby can accept recovery traffic at reduced capacity before operators scale its resources.
cards.explanation: A warm standby already runs a functional workload in the recovery Region. Extra capacity increases how much traffic it handles.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: A multi-site active/active AWS design recovers replicated data corruption by failing over to a live replica.
cards.explanation: Replication can spread corrupt changes to the other Regions. Point-in-time backups or versioned data provide an earlier recovery state.
cards.misconception: A live replica retains an uncorrupted state after corruption has replicated.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: For resilient AWS disaster recovery, AWS recommends using data plane operations for the failover steps.
cards.explanation: Recovery using data plane operations avoids dependence on control-plane configuration changes, whose availability design goals can be lower.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery can launch recovery instances from an earlier replication point in time.
cards.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery offers recovery from the latest server state or a previous point in time, so a recovery plan can select an earlier state.

source.title: What is Elastic Disaster Recovery?

cards.statement: AWS Backup re-encrypts a cross-account backup copy with the destination vault's encryption key.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup uses the destination vault's key for the copied recovery point. This separates the copy's encryption from the source vault.

source.title: Creating backup copies across AWS accounts

cards.statement: AWS Backup copies RDS continuous backups across Regions with their point-in-time recovery capability.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup copies RDS snapshots rather than the transaction logs from continuous backups. The destination copy restores the database to its snapshot state.
cards.misconception: A copied RDS continuous backup retains the source's point-in-time recovery capability.

source.title: Continuous backups and point-in-time recovery

cards.statement: AWS Backup automatically locks logically air-gapped vaults in Vault Lock compliance mode.
cards.explanation: Compliance-mode Vault Lock is built into logically air-gapped vaults. The lock enforces the configured backup retention against early deletion.

source.title: Logically air-gapped vault

cards.statement: AWS RAM can share an AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault with an organizational unit.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup shares a logically air-gapped vault through AWS RAM with individual account IDs, in the same or another organization; OUs and whole organizations are not accepted as share principals.
cards.misconception: Logically air-gapped vaults accept organizational units as share principals.

source.title: Logically air-gapped vault

cards.statement: AWS Backup can copy cold-tier recovery points across Regions to meet geographic separation requirements.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup excludes recovery points in cold tiers from cross-Region copies. Create the required Regional copy before transitioning the backup to cold storage.
cards.misconception: A recovery point remains eligible for cross-Region copying after entering cold storage.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Backup may expand storage-tier eligibility for cross-Region copies.

source.title: Creating backup copies across AWS Regions

cards.statement: An SCP Allow statement grants a member account role permission to call the allowed AWS actions.
cards.explanation: An SCP sets a ceiling for member-account permissions. IAM identity or resource policies grant access within that ceiling.
cards.misconception: An Allow in an SCP grants usable permissions to member-account roles.

source.title: Service control policies

cards.statement: An RCP can cap an external principal's access to supported resources in member accounts.
cards.explanation: RCPs constrain supported resources in member accounts even when callers belong to another organization. A resource-based Allow remains subject to the resource's RCP.

source.title: Resource control policies

cards.statement: AWS Organizations declarative policies apply to the management account as well as member accounts.
cards.explanation: Declarative policies govern service configuration across an organization, including its management account. Their scope includes tag and backup policies.

source.title: Managing organization policies with AWS Organizations

cards.statement: AWS Control Tower uses CloudFormation hooks to check resource compliance before provisioning.
cards.explanation: A proactive control checks CloudFormation resources before creation. Its hook rejects resources that fail the control's compliance checks.
cards.volatilityNote: Control Tower control implementations may evolve.

source.title: How controls work

cards.statement: AWS Control Tower sends landing zone 4.0 drift notifications to an Amazon SNS topic by default.
cards.explanation: Landing zone 4.0 sends drift notifications to Amazon EventBridge in the management account. An EventBridge rule routes those events to notification targets.
cards.misconception: Landing zone 4.0 retains the earlier direct SNS drift-notification destination.
cards.volatilityNote: Drift-notification behavior depends on the Control Tower landing zone version.

source.title: Key changes

cards.statement: AWS RAM automatically gives accounts access to an OU share when organization sharing is enabled.
cards.explanation: An OU resource share follows OU membership through AWS RAM's organization integration. The recipient accounts gain access to the share instead of exchanging invitations.

source.title: Sharing your AWS resources

cards.statement: AWS-generated cost allocation tags appear in billing reports after the management account activates them.
cards.explanation: Applying an AWS-generated tag to a resource and activating it for cost allocation are separate steps. The management account enables its use in billing reports.

source.title: Organizing and tracking costs using AWS cost allocation tags

cards.statement: A management-account AWS Budgets action can stop an EC2 instance owned by a member account.
cards.explanation: A management-account budget action can apply an SCP to another account. Its EC2 and RDS instance actions target instances in the action's own account.
cards.misconception: Management-account budget actions directly control instances in member accounts.

source.title: Configuring budget actions

cards.statement: A Savings Plan keeps discounting its former organization's consolidated bill after its owner account leaves.
cards.explanation: If a Savings Plan's owner account leaves an organization, the plan no longer applies to that organization's consolidated bill, so the remaining accounts lose its discount.
cards.misconception: An organization keeps a departed owner account's Savings Plans discounts.

source.title: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans discount sharing

cards.statement: A StackSet with service-managed permissions skips the management account, even when that account sits in a target OU.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation doesn't deploy service-managed StackSet instances to the management account, even when it belongs to a targeted OU, so that account needs its own stack for the same baseline.

source.title: Create CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation change sets can verify that custom-resource code succeeds before a stack update executes.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation change sets validate some deployment constraints, but custom-resource logic runs during execution. A successful change-set validation does not prove that this runtime code succeeds.
cards.misconception: Change-set validation executes custom-resource logic and proves the update will succeed.
cards.volatilityNote: CloudFormation pre-deployment validation coverage can evolve.

source.title: Update CloudFormation stacks using change sets

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation automatically checks nested stacks for drift when an architect checks their parent stack.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation checks a nested stack for drift when an administrator starts detection on that nested stack. A parent-stack check leaves nested-stack resources outside its inspection.
cards.misconception: Checking a parent stack for drift recursively checks its nested stacks.

source.title: Detect unmanaged configuration changes to stacks and resources

cards.statement: An AWS CloudFormation stack policy can protect a critical database from replacement during a stack update.
cards.explanation: A stack policy denies specified update actions on protected resources. This provides a safeguard against accidental replacement of a database during a broader stack update.

source.title: Prevent updates to stack resources

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation's DeletionPolicy Retain protects the old database when an update replaces the database resource.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation uses UpdateReplacePolicy Retain to preserve an old physical resource during replacement. DeletionPolicy Retain covers stack deletion or removing a resource from the template.
cards.misconception: DeletionPolicy Retain also controls retention of resources replaced during updates.

source.title: UpdateReplacePolicy attribute

cards.statement: AWS Elastic Beanstalk Standard runs a second Auto Scaling group alongside the original during an immutable deployment.
cards.explanation: An immutable deployment in Beanstalk Standard launches a second Auto Scaling group. The original instances keep running while the new fleet passes health checks.

source.title: Deploying applications to Elastic Beanstalk environments

cards.statement: An imported AWS Service Catalog portfolio can retain a product for new launches after its owner removes that product.
cards.explanation: Removing a product from a shared Service Catalog portfolio propagates to imported portfolios. Recipient accounts lose the product for future launches.
cards.misconception: An imported portfolio is an independent product catalog that survives source changes.

source.title: Sharing and Importing Portfolios

cards.statement: By default, a State Manager association reruns on a managed node that comes back online after missing a scheduled run.
cards.explanation: Besides its schedule, State Manager runs an association when a node first comes online or returns after a missed run, unless the association is set to apply only at its next cron interval.

source.title: Understanding how State Manager works

cards.statement: A cross-Region AWS CodePipeline deployment action can use the pipeline Region's S3 bucket as its artifact store.
cards.explanation: CodePipeline copies input artifacts to an artifact bucket in the cross-Region action's Region. A multi-Region pipeline needs artifact storage in its action Regions.
cards.misconception: Cross-Region pipeline actions use the pipeline Region's bucket as their artifact store.

source.title: Add a cross-region action in CodePipeline

cards.statement: A planned Aurora Global Database switchover preserves committed writes when moving the primary to another Region.
cards.explanation: Aurora waits for the target secondary to synchronize before changing the primary Region. The new primary starts from the fully synchronized data.

source.title: Using switchover or failover in Amazon Aurora Global Database

cards.statement: DynamoDB multi-Region strong consistency supports replicas in separate AWS accounts for account-level isolation.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB global tables configured for multi-Region strong consistency keep their replicas within one AWS account. The strong consistency mode excludes multi-account replication.
cards.misconception: Multi-Region strong consistency supports separating global table replicas across AWS accounts.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS may expand the account models supported by multi-Region strong consistency.

source.title: DynamoDB multi-account global tables

cards.statement: DynamoDB global tables with multi-Region eventual consistency can replicate a transaction atomically across Regions.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB provides transaction atomicity in the Region where the transaction runs. Other replicas can temporarily expose a subset of its writes.
cards.misconception: A transaction's atomicity extends to its replication across Regions in an eventually consistent global table.

source.title: Global tables core concepts

cards.statement: S3 Replication Time Control automatically publishes replication-latency metrics for cross-Region recovery.
cards.explanation: Enabling S3 Replication Time Control also enables replication metrics. Monitoring replication delay helps assess how current the recovery Region's data is.

source.title: Meeting compliance requirements with S3 Replication Time Control

cards.statement: An Amazon ElastiCache global datastore can automatically promote a secondary Region after a primary Region failure.
cards.explanation: ElastiCache promotes a secondary global datastore cluster after an explicit cross-Region failover request. A primary Region failure by itself does not trigger this promotion.
cards.misconception: A global datastore extends ElastiCache's built-in automatic failover to the secondary AWS Region.

source.title: Prerequisites and limitations

cards.statement: ARC safety rules can reject cross-Region failover updates that would leave the application's routing controls disabled.
cards.explanation: An ARC assertion rule checks the proposed routing control states against configured criteria. Operators can require an enabled control to preserve a traffic destination.

source.title: Creating safety rules for routing control

cards.statement: ARC Region switch can include application resources from separate AWS accounts in one recovery plan.
cards.explanation: Region switch supports application resources in multiple accounts and can share plans across accounts, so one team can orchestrate a Regional recovery for a multi-account application.

source.title: Region switch in ARC

cards.statement: After origin failover, Amazon CloudFront pins later cache misses to the secondary with default origin priority.
cards.explanation: CloudFront tries the primary origin again for a later cache miss under default origin priority. A previous request's failover leaves the primary's priority intact.
cards.misconception: Origin failover switches later origin requests persistently to the secondary until a separate failback.

source.title: Optimize high availability with CloudFront origin failover

cards.statement: AWS Fault Injection Service pauses DynamoDB global table replication to simulate isolation of a recovery Region.
cards.explanation: The replication-pause action stops replication into and out of the targeted Region. Other Regions continue replicating with each other.

source.title: Cross-Region: Connectivity

cards.statement: A permissions boundary requires an Allow for a resource policy grant directly to a same-account IAM role session.
cards.explanation: An implicit deny in a permissions boundary does not constrain permissions granted directly to a same-account IAM role session by a resource policy.
cards.misconception: A boundary's implicit denial limits direct resource-based grants to an IAM role session.

source.title: Permissions boundaries for IAM entities

cards.statement: iam:PassRole requires the service role and the target AWS service to belong to the same account.
cards.explanation: A centralized deployment design passes a role local to the target service's account. A role owned by another account is outside the scope of iam:PassRole.

source.title: Grant a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service

cards.statement: A security group rule can reference a security group in a peered VPC that is in another Region.
cards.explanation: Security group references across a VPC peering connection work only when both VPCs are in the same Region, in the same or another account. For an inter-Region peer, rules use the peer VPC's CIDR block.
cards.misconception: Security group references work across an inter-Region VPC peering connection.

source.title: Update your security groups to reference peer security groups

cards.statement: An AWS Firewall Manager policy for an OU can automatically cover new accounts added to that OU.
cards.explanation: Selecting an OU keeps the policy scope aligned with its membership. Firewall Manager evaluates newly added accounts against that policy.

source.title: Creating an AWS Firewall Manager policy

cards.statement: AWS Shield Advanced requires a protected resource's Amazon Route 53 health check for proactive engagement.
cards.explanation: AWS Shield Advanced proactive engagement uses resource health to decide whether a detected attack warrants contact from the Shield Response Team.

source.title: Setting up proactive engagement for the SRT to contact you directly

cards.statement: An AWS managed KMS key can support direct cross-account decryption for a shared application data store.
cards.explanation: An AWS managed KMS key restricts cryptographic use to its owning account. Select a customer managed key for direct cross-account decryption.
cards.misconception: An AWS managed KMS key is suitable for direct cross-account access to shared encrypted application data.

source.title: AWS KMS keys

cards.statement: An Amazon S3 bucket policy can restrict cross-account access to requests through designated VPC endpoints.
cards.explanation: An endpoint condition in the bucket policy rejects requests arriving through other network paths, even when an external account otherwise has permission.

source.title: Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies

cards.statement: AWS Secrets Manager can propagate a rotated primary secret's new value to replicas in other Regions.
cards.explanation: Rotation runs on the primary secret, and Secrets Manager distributes the resulting value to its replicas. This keeps regional copies aligned with the primary credential.

source.title: Replicate AWS Secrets Manager secrets across Regions

cards.statement: A Network Load Balancer TLS listener meets end-to-end encryption needs with a TCP target group.
cards.explanation: A TLS listener decrypts the client connection. For client-to-target TLS passthrough, a TCP listener forwards encrypted traffic for the target to decrypt.
cards.misconception: A TLS listener keeps traffic encrypted between the load balancer and a TCP target group.

source.title: Listeners for your Network Load Balancers

cards.statement: ARC zonal autoshift can move an application's traffic out of an Availability Zone where its resources are healthy.
cards.explanation: AWS starts an autoshift from its own telemetry of an Availability Zone impairment and does not inspect individual resource health, so AWS recommends pre-scaling capacity in the other zones.

source.title: Zonal autoshift in ARC

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling automatically registers instances with its load balancer during a launch hook's wait.
cards.explanation: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling waits for the launch hook to finish before registering the instance with its load balancer. The architect uses this pause to complete application bootstrapping.
cards.misconception: The launch lifecycle hook prepares an instance after Auto Scaling has registered it for traffic.

source.title: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can target Amazon SQS backlog per instance for workers with a queue delay requirement.
cards.explanation: Backlog per instance relates queued work to available worker capacity. The architect chooses its target using acceptable delay and average message processing time.

source.title: Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS

cards.statement: An Amazon SNS subscription can use a dead-letter queue owned by a different account in the organization.
cards.explanation: An Amazon SNS subscription's dead-letter queue belongs to the same account and Region as the subscription. Organization membership leaves this ownership requirement in place.
cards.misconception: Organization membership permits a central account to own another account's SNS subscription dead-letter queue.

source.title: Amazon SNS dead-letter queues

cards.statement: AWS Step Functions automatically retries failed order-processing tasks using its default workflow retry policy.
cards.explanation: AWS Step Functions supplies no default task retry policy. The architect specifies which task errors to retry in the workflow.
cards.misconception: Step Functions automatically gives new workflow tasks a retry policy.

source.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

cards.statement: After retries fail, AWS Step Functions sends matching task errors to a compensation branch configured in a catcher.
cards.explanation: A catcher routes matching task errors to a fallback state defined by the architect. That path can perform compensation, such as releasing inventory reserved earlier.

source.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

cards.statement: When a Multi-AZ Redis OSS primary fails, Amazon ElastiCache promotes the replica with the least replication lag.
cards.explanation: ElastiCache promotes the most current replica, which minimizes data lost to asynchronous replication. Writes resume within seconds through the unchanged primary endpoint.

source.title: Minimizing downtime in ElastiCache by using Multi-AZ with Valkey and Redis OSS

cards.statement: For shared Capacity Reservations, Amazon EC2 counts consumer instances against the consumer account's On-Demand quota.
cards.explanation: Instances launched into a shared Capacity Reservation consume the reservation owner's On-Demand Instance quota. The central capacity owner plans quota headroom for consumer launches.
cards.misconception: A consuming account's own On-Demand quota is charged for instances using another account's reserved capacity.

source.title: Shared Capacity Reservations

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 IP-based routing can steer hybrid clients by address range for records in a private hosted zone.
cards.explanation: Route 53 IP-based routing applies to public hosted zones. An architect chooses a different routing approach for records in a private hosted zone.
cards.misconception: IP-based routing policies work in private hosted zones for hybrid client networks.

source.title: IP-based routing

cards.statement: DynamoDB Accelerator can route strongly consistent reads to DynamoDB while a multi-AZ cache holds the requested item.
cards.explanation: DAX forwards strongly consistent reads to DynamoDB rather than serving them from its cache. A multi-AZ DAX deployment still leaves strict-freshness reads dependent on DynamoDB.

source.title: DAX and DynamoDB consistency models

cards.statement: An ElastiCache for Redis OSS cluster with multiple shards spreads write-heavy traffic across several primaries.
cards.explanation: Cluster mode enabled distributes Redis OSS data across shards, with a primary accepting writes for its shard. Additional write endpoints help a design scale a write-heavy cache.

source.title: Replication: Valkey and Redis OSS Cluster Mode Disabled vs. Enabled

cards.statement: Amazon RDS for MySQL adds read replicas to a DB instance automatically when the instance's read traffic grows.
cards.explanation: RDS doesn't autoscale read replicas: an architect creates and deletes them, so a design with spiky read demand needs its own scaling logic.
cards.misconception: RDS read replicas scale out automatically with read demand.

source.title: Working with DB instance read replicas

cards.statement: AWS recommends Amazon EFS Max I/O for the lowest per-operation latency across a regional compute fleet.
cards.explanation: General Purpose provides lower per-operation latency than Max I/O. AWS recommends General Purpose for EFS file systems, including designs with strict file-operation latency requirements.
cards.misconception: Max I/O is AWS's recommendation when the lowest file-operation latency is required.

source.title: Amazon EFS performance

cards.statement: Amazon MemoryDB can replace a cache plus a separate durable database as a microservice's primary data store.
cards.explanation: MemoryDB serves data from memory and stores it durably across Availability Zones in a Multi-AZ transactional log, so one service can act as a high-performance primary database.

source.title: What is MemoryDB

cards.statement: DynamoDB adaptive capacity can isolate a single heavily accessed item on its own partition to reduce throttling.
cards.explanation: Adaptive capacity rebalances partitions so frequently accessed items stop sharing one. An isolated item still gets at most one partition's maximum throughput.

source.title: DynamoDB burst and adaptive capacity

cards.statement: Database Savings Plans can cover eligible usage after an application moves from Amazon RDS to Amazon DynamoDB.
cards.explanation: Database Savings Plans apply across supported database services. A modernization can move eligible usage from RDS to DynamoDB while the same spending commitment remains useful.
cards.volatilityNote: Database Savings Plans coverage and eligible usage can evolve.

source.title: Savings Plans types

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 zonal Reserved Instance can reserve capacity for other accounts on its consolidated bill.
cards.explanation: EC2 confines a zonal Reserved Instance's capacity reservation to its owning account. Consolidated billing does not share that capacity.
cards.misconception: Consolidated billing shares a zonal Reserved Instance's reserved capacity across accounts.

source.title: How Reserved Instance discounts are applied

cards.statement: S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a retrieval fee when an application reads an object from its Infrequent Access tier.
cards.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fees; it charges a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, which suits data with unknown or changing access patterns.
cards.misconception: Intelligent-Tiering bills retrievals from its infrequent tiers like S3 Standard-IA.

source.title: Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes

cards.statement: CloudWatch cross-account observability can link telemetry from several Regions directly to a single monitoring sink.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch cross-account observability links source and monitoring accounts within one Region. A multi-Region observability design needs an arrangement beyond a single regional link.
cards.misconception: A single cross-account observability sink accepts source telemetry across Regions.

source.title: CloudWatch cross-account observability

cards.statement: CloudWatch Logs centralization automatically copies new logs from several accounts and Regions into a central account.
cards.explanation: Centralization rules select source accounts and Regions and a destination within the organization. Copies in the destination support analysis of workloads spanning those sources.

source.title: Cross-account cross-Region log centralization

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge can start a Systems Manager Automation runbook when a CloudWatch alarm reports instance failure.
cards.explanation: EventBridge targets include Systems Manager Automation runbooks. An alarm-driven rule starts a chosen recovery workflow, replacing a manual response to the monitored failure.

source.title: Sample scenarios: Systems Manager targets in Amazon EventBridge rules

cards.statement: AWS Systems Manager Automation requires an execution role in each target account for centralized fleet remediation.
cards.explanation: The central Automation account uses an administration role, while execution roles authorize work in targeted accounts. This separates orchestration permissions from the permissions used on fleet resources.

source.title: Running automations in multiple AWS Regions and accounts

cards.statement: AWS Fault Injection Service stops an experiment when its configured CloudWatch latency alarm enters ALARM.
cards.explanation: A stop condition uses a CloudWatch alarm to guard the workload's steady state. Crossing the chosen latency threshold ends the experiment before it continues injecting faults.

source.title: Stop conditions for AWS FIS

cards.statement: AWS Fault Injection Service adds newly matching instances to a running experiment as an Auto Scaling fleet grows.
cards.explanation: AWS Fault Injection Service resolves targets at experiment start and keeps that selection for the experiment. Newly launched matching instances remain outside that selected target set.
cards.misconception: Fault Injection Service refreshes tag-based targets throughout a running experiment.

source.title: Targets for AWS FIS

cards.statement: The Rolling policy in AWS Elastic Beanstalk Standard preserves full serving capacity during an application deployment.
cards.explanation: The Rolling policy takes the current batch out of service, reducing serving capacity during deployment. An architect accounts for this reduction when the workload has a capacity requirement.
cards.misconception: Standard rolling deployments maintain the fleet's full serving capacity while updating batches.

source.title: Deployment policies and settings

cards.statement: AWS CodeDeploy automatically reverses configuration changes made by deployment scripts when it rolls back a release.
cards.explanation: CodeDeploy redeploys an earlier application revision but leaves script side effects to the application team. A rollback plan needs explicit logic for undoing those configuration changes.
cards.misconception: CodeDeploy rollback automatically reconciles configuration changes performed by deployment scripts.

source.title: Redeploy and roll back a deployment with CodeDeploy

cards.statement: A CloudWatch composite alarm can reduce duplicate notifications from related failures across monitored source accounts.
cards.explanation: A composite alarm evaluates combined alarm states and issues an aggregate notification. With cross-account observability, its underlying alarms can monitor metrics from linked source accounts.

source.title: Composite alarms

cards.statement: AWS Config automatically rechecks a resource's current compliance before running its configured automatic remediation.
cards.explanation: AWS Config starts automatic remediation from a compliance snapshot that can be stale. A resource fixed since that snapshot can still receive the remediation.
cards.misconception: Automatic remediation refreshes compliance immediately before acting on a resource.

source.title: Setting Up Auto Remediation for AWS Config

cards.statement: An AWS Config organization conformance pack protects centrally deployed rules from member-account edits.
cards.explanation: Organization conformance packs deploy centrally controlled Config rules and remediation actions. AWS Config prevents member accounts from editing those underlying rules.

source.title: Managing Conformance Packs for AWS Config Across all Accounts in Your Organization

cards.statement: AWS Secrets Manager alternating-user rotation keeps the previous user's database credentials valid after rotation.
cards.explanation: Alternating-user rotation maintains two working database logins. Applications reading the current secret during rotation receive valid credentials, reducing authentication failures in a highly available workload.

source.title: Lambda function rotation strategies

cards.statement: An IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer for an organization can review permission activity across AWS Regions.
cards.explanation: Unused access analysis uses IAM activity across the organization. Its findings are independent of the analyzer's Region, so a regional analyzer can support an organization-wide permissions review.

source.title: Create an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer

cards.statement: IAM service last accessed data confirms successful service requests when an architect audits a role's permissions.
cards.explanation: IAM service last accessed data includes denied attempts as well as successful requests. CloudTrail logs provide the authoritative evidence of whether a particular request succeeded.
cards.misconception: A service last accessed entry proves that the corresponding API request was authorized and successful.

source.title: Refine permissions in AWS using last accessed information

cards.statement: By default, Amazon Inspector stops rescanning an ECR image not pushed or used within the configured re-scan durations.
cards.explanation: Inspector rescans an ECR image while its push date or, in the default mode, its last-in-use date is within the configured durations; after that it marks the image inactive and closes its findings.

source.title: Configuring the Amazon ECR re-scan duration

cards.statement: Amazon Macie's new-account enrollment setting can also enable Macie for existing organization accounts.
cards.explanation: Macie's automatic enablement setting affects accounts that subsequently join the organization. The delegated administrator separately adds existing accounts to close their coverage gap.
cards.misconception: Turning on automatic enablement for new accounts also enrolls the organization's existing accounts.

source.title: Integrating and configuring an organization in Macie

cards.statement: Amazon Detective depends on active Amazon GuardDuty membership to investigate an existing account's activity.
cards.explanation: Detective works in an account with GuardDuty disabled. An architect can add its account-activity analysis independently when improving an existing investigation process.
cards.misconception: GuardDuty membership is a prerequisite for adding Detective's investigation capability.

source.title: Amazon Detective FAQs

cards.statement: An AWS CloudTrail organization trail can record S3 object deletions by default for a central access audit.
cards.explanation: A CloudTrail trail leaves data events unselected by default. An architect explicitly includes S3 object data events to trace object deletions during an access audit.
cards.misconception: The default event selection in an organization trail includes S3 object deletion activity.

source.title: Logging data events

cards.statement: A shared EC2 cluster placement group can improve node-to-node latency for applications spanning AWS accounts.
cards.explanation: AWS RAM shares a cluster placement group with other accounts. Participants place interdependent instances in the shared group and connect their VPCs to gain its latency benefits.

source.title: Shared placement groups

cards.statement: Launching several instance types into one EC2 cluster placement group improves the odds that the launch finds capacity.
cards.explanation: AWS allows mixed instance types in a cluster placement group but says this reduces the chance that the required capacity is available; it recommends one instance type launched in a single request.
cards.misconception: Mixing instance types widens the capacity available to a cluster placement group launch.

source.title: Placement strategies for your placement groups

cards.statement: For topology-aware replication, Amazon EC2 gives each partition in a partition placement group distinct racks.
cards.explanation: Different partitions in a partition placement group use distinct racks. A topology-aware application uses partition information to keep data replicas apart from shared hardware failures.

source.title: Placement strategies for your placement groups

cards.statement: With instance weights, an Auto Scaling group keeps its current capacity at or below the desired capacity in units.
cards.explanation: Current capacity can exceed desired capacity when a launched instance carries more units than remain to be filled, so AWS advises a desired capacity two to three times the largest weight.
cards.misconception: A weighted Auto Scaling group never overshoots its desired capacity units.

source.title: Configure an Auto Scaling group to use instance weights

cards.statement: AWS Global Accelerator can improve a global UDP application's network path while keeping its existing regional hosts.
cards.explanation: Global Accelerator carries application traffic from nearby edge locations over the AWS network to regional endpoints. Existing EC2 instances or load balancers remain the application hosts.

source.title: How AWS Global Accelerator works

cards.statement: CloudFront Functions can replace an origin's remote authorization lookup by calling that external service at the edge.
cards.explanation: CloudFront Functions runs with no network access. An edge design that calls an external authorization service needs a runtime that provides network access.
cards.misconception: CloudFront Functions supports remote service calls for moving existing authorization processing to the edge.

source.title: Differences between CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge

cards.statement: For cache-heavy sites, CloudFront limits origin-request Lambda@Edge execution to cache misses, sparing cached responses.
cards.explanation: An origin-request trigger runs when CloudFront forwards a request to the origin. Cache hits avoid invoking the function and adding its processing latency.

source.title: CloudFront events that can trigger a Lambda@Edge function

cards.statement: CloudWatch Database Insights can separate DB load by wait type to help architects identify an RDS fleet's bottlenecks.
cards.explanation: Database Insights filters database load by waits across a monitored RDS fleet. The wait breakdown helps an architect target the bottleneck before changing instance capacity.

source.title: Monitoring Amazon RDS databases with CloudWatch Database Insights

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling's capacity-optimized Spot strategy selects replacement types by the fleet's priority order.
cards.explanation: The capacity-optimized strategy selects Spot pools using real-time available capacity. Instance-type ordering belongs to capacity-optimized-prioritized, which still prioritizes capacity.
cards.misconception: The capacity-optimized strategy follows the fleet's configured instance-type ordering during replacement.

source.title: Allocation strategies for multiple instance types

cards.statement: When Elastic Load Balancing reports every instance unhealthy, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can throttle their replacement.
cards.explanation: If ELB health checks report all instances unhealthy while the load balancer is InService, Auto Scaling might mark fewer of them unhealthy at a time, leaving time to fix the fault before the whole group is replaced.

source.title: About the health checks for your Auto Scaling group

cards.statement: Amazon RDS Proxy can replay an in-flight transaction automatically after a database failover interrupts it.
cards.explanation: A failover cancels a connection in the middle of a transaction or SQL statement through RDS Proxy. Application recovery logic handles the interrupted work rather than expecting the proxy to replay it.
cards.misconception: RDS Proxy automatically replays transactions interrupted by database failover.

source.title: RDS Proxy concepts and terminology

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB automatically creates a new table when a team restores corrupted production data to a point in time.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB restores a historical recovery point into a new table. A recovery plan moves the application's reads and writes to that restored table instead of expecting an in-place rollback.

source.title: Restoring a DynamoDB table to a point in time

cards.statement: Updating a Service Quotas request template requests its new quota values for existing accounts in the organization.
cards.explanation: A quota request template requests its values for accounts created in the organization after association. Updating it leaves existing accounts' quotas unchanged, so they need their own increase requests.
cards.misconception: Request template updates apply to existing member accounts.

source.title: Using Service Quotas request templates

cards.statement: An instance reuse policy makes Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling return scaled-in instances to the group's warm pool.
cards.explanation: An instance reuse policy sends scaled-in instances back to the warm pool. A workload with lengthy initialization reuses prepared instances when demand grows again.

source.title: Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools

cards.statement: Amazon CloudWatch action based recovery preserves EC2 instance store data while moving an instance to a new host.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch action based recovery loses data on the instance's local store. A workload that uses local data needs a recovery plan that rebuilds it from a durable source.
cards.misconception: Moving an EC2 instance through CloudWatch action based recovery preserves its instance store data.

source.title: Automatic instance recovery

cards.statement: AWS Compute Optimizer can assess performance risk before teams downsize over-provisioned EC2 instances in a fleet.
cards.explanation: Compute Optimizer evaluates recommended instance types against the workload's resource demands. Its performance risk assessment helps teams evaluate a cost reduction before changing fleet capacity.

source.title: Viewing EC2 instance recommendations

cards.statement: A CloudWatch billing alarm compares projected month-end charges with its threshold to prompt cost intervention.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch billing alarms compare current estimated charges with the threshold. Their billing metric reflects accrued costs rather than a projection of the month's final bill.
cards.misconception: A CloudWatch billing alarm evaluates a month-end cost forecast instead of charges accrued so far.

source.title: Create a billing alarm to monitor your estimated AWS charges

cards.statement: Deleting an older incremental Amazon EBS snapshot removes block data that the volume's newer snapshots still reference.
cards.explanation: EBS removes only data referenced exclusively by the deleted snapshot and keeps blocks that later snapshots use, so deleting old snapshots might not reduce storage costs.
cards.misconception: Deleting an older snapshot frees all of the blocks it stored.

source.title: Delete an Amazon EBS snapshot

cards.statement: AWS's relocate strategy can move an existing Amazon RDS production database between AWS accounts.
cards.explanation: AWS includes moving existing resources between accounts in the relocate strategy. A portfolio migration can use relocation to change an RDS database's account placement while preserving its architecture.

source.title: About the migration strategies

cards.statement: AWS classifies moving SQL Server to Amazon RDS for SQL Server with unchanged application code as refactoring.
cards.explanation: AWS treats moving SQL Server to RDS for SQL Server as replatforming. The move changes the database operating platform while preserving the application's architecture.
cards.misconception: Moving an existing database to a managed version of the same engine counts as refactoring.

source.title: About the migration strategies

cards.statement: For large AWS migrations, AWS recommends refactoring applications during migration rather than after the move.
cards.explanation: For large migrations, AWS recommends rehosting, relocating or replatforming first and modernizing afterward. Refactoring during the move adds complexity across the application portfolio.
cards.misconception: AWS recommends combining large-scale migration and application refactoring into the same move.

source.title: About the migration strategies

cards.statement: AWS wave planning guidance filters shared services such as Active Directory out of dependency data before grouping.
cards.explanation: Shared services such as Active Directory, backup and monitoring connect to almost everything and would glue the portfolio into one group, so the guidance excludes them when deriving dependency groups.

source.title: Wave planning

cards.statement: AWS recommends AWS Transform over AWS Migration Hub when an organization starts a new migration project.
cards.explanation: AWS recommends starting new migration projects in AWS Transform. Migration Hub remains available to existing customers completing ongoing projects.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Transform capabilities and AWS migration-tool recommendations continue to evolve.

source.title: AWS Migration Hub availability change

cards.statement: AWS Transform MGN automatically replicates source disk changes while source applications continue serving users.
cards.explanation: MGN continuously copies changed disk blocks before cutover. Keeping the AWS copy current while applications run leaves the final cutover to synchronize the remaining changes.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Transform MGN migration capabilities continue to evolve.

source.title: What Is AWS Transform MGN?

cards.statement: AWS DMS bidirectional replication resolves conflicting updates made to the same rows on both databases.
cards.explanation: DMS bidirectional replication runs two tasks with loopback prevention but has no conflict detection or resolution, so a fallback design keeps each data element written on one side only.
cards.misconception: Bidirectional DMS replication works as a multi-master solution with conflict resolution.

source.title: Creating tasks for ongoing replication using AWS DMS

cards.statement: AWS Data Transfer Terminal lets migration teams upload a dataset from their own devices at an AWS facility.
cards.explanation: Customers bring their data storage devices to a reserved Data Transfer Terminal facility. The facility supplies a network-ready location for transferring the dataset to AWS.

source.title: What is Data Transfer Terminal?

cards.statement: AD Connector caches directory data in AWS so Amazon WorkSpaces users can sign in while the on-premises link is down.
cards.explanation: AD Connector is a directory gateway that redirects requests to on-premises Active Directory without caching any information in the cloud, so sign-ins depend on connectivity to that directory.
cards.misconception: AD Connector keeps a cached directory copy in AWS that covers connectivity outages.

source.title: AD Connector

cards.statement: AWS Fargate can host an unchanged workload that requires privileged containers for host-level operations.
cards.explanation: Fargate excludes privileged containers and host-level access. A migrated workload that retains this requirement needs a container hosting option with the necessary privileges.
cards.misconception: Fargate supports privileged containers needed by an unchanged workload.

source.title: Fargate security considerations for Amazon ECS

cards.statement: Amazon ECS Anywhere can register on-premises service tasks with Elastic Load Balancing through ECS service integration.
cards.explanation: ECS Anywhere excludes ECS service load balancing for external instances. A migrated on-premises web service needs a separate approach for distributing inbound traffic.
cards.misconception: ECS service integration registers ECS Anywhere tasks with Elastic Load Balancing.

source.title: Amazon ECS clusters for external instances

cards.statement: EKS Anywhere keeps a cluster's control plane on customer infrastructure for an application confined to the data center.
cards.explanation: An EKS Anywhere cluster runs entirely on the customer's infrastructure. The customer manages its control plane, which fits a workload needing local Kubernetes cluster operation.

source.title: Frequently Asked Questions

cards.statement: Amazon ECR automatically deletes cross-Region image replicas when the source account deletes the original image.
cards.explanation: ECR replication propagates images but leaves deletion independent at the destination. Deleting a source image therefore preserves an existing replica in another Region.
cards.misconception: An ECR replication rule synchronizes image deletions across Regions.

source.title: Private image replication in Amazon ECR

cards.statement: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP can serve one volume over NFS and SMB to preserve a migrated mixed-platform workload.
cards.explanation: FSx for ONTAP permits concurrent NFS and SMB access to the same volume. Existing Linux and Windows applications can keep their file-access protocols while sharing the migrated data.

source.title: Managing FSx for ONTAP volumes

cards.statement: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server can join a self-managed Active Directory domain directly for migrated file shares.
cards.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server joins the existing self-managed domain at creation. A file-share migration can retain its on-premises directory and user identities.
tags: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

source.title: Using a self-managed Microsoft Active Directory

cards.statement: For cross-account Amazon EFS access, architects use Availability Zone IDs to match each client to a local mount target.
cards.explanation: Availability Zone names can map differently across accounts. Matching the client's and mount target's Availability Zone IDs identifies the same physical zone for cross-account EFS access.

source.title: Mounting EFS file systems from another VPC

cards.statement: Volume Gateway stored volumes keep the primary data in Amazon S3 and hold a local copy of frequently accessed subsets.
cards.explanation: Stored volumes keep the full dataset on premises and asynchronously back up point-in-time snapshots to Amazon S3; cached volumes are the option that keeps primary data in S3.
cards.misconception: Stored volumes use Amazon S3 as primary storage with a local cache.

source.title: What is Volume Gateway?

cards.statement: Aurora MySQL can receive binary log replication from an on-premises MySQL source during a staged database migration.
cards.explanation: Aurora MySQL accepts binlog replication from a MySQL database outside RDS. The Aurora cluster can receive source updates before the application moves to the new database.

source.title: Replication between Aurora and MySQL or between Aurora and another Aurora DB cluster (binary log replication)

cards.statement: Asynchronous AWS Step Functions Express Workflows can guarantee exactly-once execution for payment processing.
cards.explanation: Asynchronous Express Workflows use at-least-once execution, so a workflow can run more than once. Payment actions need idempotency to tolerate duplicate execution.
cards.misconception: Asynchronous Express Workflows guarantee exactly-once execution for payment actions.

source.title: Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

cards.statement: Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ supports XA distributed transactions for JMS applications leaving a commercial broker.
cards.explanation: Amazon MQ supports standard JMS features, including JMS and distributed (XA) transactions, so an application leaving IBM MQ or TIBCO EMS can keep its transaction semantics with minimal code changes.

source.title: What is the Amazon MQ migration guide?

cards.statement: An Amazon EventBridge replay can name an event bus other than its archive's source bus as the replay destination.
cards.explanation: Archived events can be replayed only to the archive's source event bus. A replay can be limited to chosen rules on that bus, whose targets then receive the events.
cards.misconception: A replay can deliver archived events to any event bus, including one in another account.

source.title: Archiving and replaying events in Amazon EventBridge

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS transaction can atomically commit a business update and publish its matching Amazon SQS message.
cards.explanation: An RDS write and direct SQS publication are separate operations. A transactional outbox saves the change and an event record in one database transaction, then a publisher sends committed events.
cards.misconception: A database transaction also atomically commits its application's direct SQS publication.

source.title: Transactional outbox pattern

cards.statement: An eligible Aurora Serverless v2 cluster with a minimum of 0 ACUs lets idle instances pause automatically.
cards.explanation: A minimum of 0 ACUs enables auto-pause on supported Aurora engines and compatible cluster configurations. Idle eligible instances pause, and a later connection request resumes them.
cards.volatilityNote: Auto-pause eligibility and supported engine versions can evolve.

source.title: Scaling to Zero ACUs with automatic pause and resume for Aurora serverless

cards.statement: Amazon ECS Express Mode automatically creates a web application's supporting resources in the customer's AWS account.
cards.explanation: Express Mode configures the supporting resources in the customer's account. Platform teams retain visibility and access to the infrastructure behind a modernized web application.
cards.volatilityNote: Express Mode infrastructure orchestration and management features can evolve.

source.title: Amazon ECS Express Mode

cards.statement: Amazon ECS Service Connect automatically adds new endpoint discovery to existing client tasks in its namespace.
cards.explanation: Existing Service Connect client tasks retain the endpoint configuration from their deployment. The application team redeploys the client service to discover a newly added endpoint.
cards.misconception: Existing Service Connect client tasks automatically receive newly added endpoint discovery configuration.

source.title: Amazon ECS Service Connect components

cards.statement: AWS Transform can turn an existing application's source code into a container deployment for Amazon ECS.
cards.explanation: AWS Transform accepts application source code, builds container images and generates deployment infrastructure. This delegates containerization work when modernizing an application for ECS.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS Transform containerization capabilities and deployment workflows can evolve.

source.title: Source code containerization

cards.statement: Amazon Neptune preserves the RDF data model and SPARQL query language when an existing graph application modernizes.
cards.explanation: Neptune supports RDF graphs queried with SPARQL. An existing RDF application can retain that data and query model while its team adopts a managed graph database.

source.title: What Is Amazon Neptune?
